Meddle
MED-ul
v.
Old French medler, a variant of mesler, to mix, from Latin miscere—the root of mix and miscellaneous. To meddle is to mix oneself into what one was not mixed into.

Biblical Definition

To meddle is to mix yourself into a matter that is not yours, and Proverbs treats it as a mark of folly rather than of zeal. The central image is unforgettable: He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears (Prov 26:17)—a man who was merely walking past, who reaches into a fight he had no part in, and who now cannot let go without being bitten. Proverbs contrasts it with honor: It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling (Prov 20:3). Ceasing is the honorable move; the fool cannot leave it alone. There is also a political form: My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change (Prov 24:21)—keep clear of the perpetually agitated, the men whose settled posture is overthrow. And there is a sober historical example. Josiah, a genuinely good king, rides out against Pharaoh Necho, who sends word, What have I to do with thee, thou king of Judah? ... forbear thee from meddling with God, who is with me, that he destroy thee not (2 Chr 35:21). Josiah meddles anyway and dies of it. That is the warning Proverbs is making practical: meddling is not always the vice of a bad man. It is often the last mistake of a good one who could not stay out of a quarrel God had not assigned him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MEDDLE as to have to do with; to interpose or interfere officiously; to take part in the concerns of others which do not belong to one, and where one has no business.

expand to see more

MEDDLE, v.i. — To have to do; to take part; to interpose or interfere. Usually followed by with.

MEDDLE, v.i. — To interpose or interfere officiously; to act in the concerns of others without being invited or having a right. Every fool will be meddling (Prov 20:3).

Key Scripture

Proverbs 20:3 — "It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling."

Proverbs 26:17 — "He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears."

Proverbs 24:21 — "My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:"

Modern Corruption

The internet turned meddling into a civic duty—every distant quarrel presented as a matter requiring your position—so that a man now spends his attention on fights he cannot affect and neglects the field actually assigned to him.

expand to see more

The economics are simple: platforms profit from engagement, and nothing engages like a quarrel. So a man is served, all day, strife belonging not to him—other people's marriages, other cities' politics, other churches' scandals—each framed as something on which silence would be complicity. Proverbs 26:17 describes exactly this posture, and the trap in it: the passer-by grabs the ears, and now letting go costs blood. Anyone who has tried to exit a public argument knows the verse is literal.

The needful distinction is between meddling and duty. Scripture commands intervention in specific places: deliver those drawn unto death, rebuke a brother, defend the fatherless and the widow, restore a man overtaken in a fault. Those are assigned fields, and the assignment usually comes with proximity—a brother, a neighbor, a household, a flock. Meddling is what happens when a man skips the assigned field for the unassigned one, and the tell is that meddling costs him nothing but attention and gratifies him immediately, whereas the strife that actually belongs to him is close, slow, and thankless.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew garah, to stir up strife, and arab, to mix oneself in—the two ways a man gets into a quarrel that was not his.

expand to see more

Hebrew arab (H6148) — to mix, mingle, give oneself as a pledge; hence to intermeddle in another's affairs (Prov 14:10; 20:19; 24:21).

Hebrew garah (H1624) — to stir up, provoke, engage in strife; used of meddling in a quarrel and of provoking a war (Deut 2:5; Prov 15:18; 28:4; 2 Chr 35:21).

Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, reveal; the companion sin of Prov 20:19, the talebearer who reveals secrets, with whom one is told not to meddle.

Usage

"Like one that taketh a dog by the ears—grabbing is easy; letting go costs blood."

"It is an honour for a man to cease from strife—ceasing is the honorable move."

"Josiah meddled with a quarrel God had not assigned him and died of it (2 Chr 35:21)."
